Private-pay rates for small shared-room PCHs — no public source. Whether the 2025 proposed amendments to Chapter 111-8-62 (presented to the Board 2/13/2025) were finally adopted and when they took effect; whether PCH (under 25 beds) staffing ratios were changed by the May 21, 2025 amendments. Full text of Rules 111-8-63-.06 (permit) beyond subsection 6 and 111-8-63-.08 (administration) — not retrievable from the official site.

Local occupational tax certificate amounts for specific counties/cities; the $25/month line is an operator estimate inside a secondary $10–$1,000+ range.

occupancy.rationale: No Georgia occupancy or bed-utilization data was found from an official source. The 85% default is an operator planning assumption, deliberately cautious because one vacancy in a small home is 4–17% of census. The 75% conservative case matters most for 6- and 16-bed homes. New homes ramp up from a small first admission (CCSP enrollment takes about 2–4 months per a secondary source, but private-pay admissions are the modeled revenue).

configurations.label: 6-bed Personal Care Home, 100% private pay (paid administrator)
configurations.notes: Smallest common Georgia model (PCH 2–24 beds, Rule 111-8-62). Priced at the $4,395 A Place for Mom Georgia median [S48] because a shared room in a residential home likely prices below the CareScout private-one-bedroom median of $5,300 [S30]; both are benchmarks, not small-home price surveys, and the $4,395 median covers all Georgia assisted living move-ins, not small PCHs specifically. A PCH may not provide assisted living care without an ALC license [S9]. Medicaid ALS revenue is not modeled because no 2026 per-diem was found. Staffing: 1 awake direct care staff per 15 residents waking / 1 per 25 non-waking for homes under 25 beds [S11] means one awake staff member 24/7 (730 hrs). The administrator is budgeted at a salary; if the owner is the administrator, that line is the owner's pay. With a paid administrator this home is structurally unprofitable at this price: at 100% occupancy revenue is $26,370 a month against about $30,700 of listed costs, a loss of about $4,300 a month before any vacancy, and it does not cover its costs at 85% occupancy either.

configurations.notes: ALC licensed under Rule 111-8-63 (25+ residents). sections.executive_summary:
Georgia does not use the single label "assisted living facility" for every home. A **Personal Care Home (PCH)** is licensed under Rule 111-8-62 and covers homes of 2 to 24 beds. An **Assisted Living Community (ALC)** is a personal care home serving 25 or more residents that is licensed to provide assisted living care, under Rule 111-8-63 [S1][S15][S16]. A home licensed only as a PCH may not provide assisted living care [S9]. Both are licensed by the Department of Community Health (DCH), Healthcare Facility Regulation Division [S8][S14]. DCH's PCH program reports overseeing 2,910 facilities of mixed types serving roughly 55,000 residents. The page is undated, and the figure does not separate PCHs from ALCs [S14]. Georgia's 65+ population is 16.7% of 11,302,748 residents [S47], which is roughly 1.9 million people (simple arithmetic, not a published count).

Most of the revenue in this report is private pay. CareScout's 2025 Georgia median for an assisted living community is $5,300 a month ($63,600 a year). That figure is for a private one-bedroom unit in an AL community, and the U.S. median is $6,200 [S30]. For PCH configurations the model uses a lower $4,395 monthly median from an A Place for Mom-based report [S48]. A second page on the same site gives a conflicting $4,752 average [S49], and neither source measures small shared-room homes. Medicaid pays through the Elderly and Disabled Waiver Program (CCSP and SOURCE), whose Alternative Living Services cover 24-hour personal care supervision in licensed PCHs [S20][S21][S22]. The waiver does not pay room and board. The resident pays it from SSI, and secondary sources put that amount at $768 a month from January 1, 2026 [S24][S25]. **No 2026 Medicaid per-diem for ALS was found, so no Medicaid revenue is modeled and every configuration is private pay.**

**What the model shows at 85% occupancy.** The best result is the 24-bed PCH, which nets about $19,025 a month (21.2% margin), breaks even at 63.7% occupancy, first turns profitable in month 6, and needs about $142,027 in cash. The 16-bed PCH nets about $4,040 a month (6.8%) and breaks even at 78.2%. The 12-bed PCH nets about $1,257 (2.8%) and breaks even at 82.2%. The 30-bed ALC nets about $6,611 (4.9%), breaks even at 80.2%, and needs about $435,837. The 6-bed PCH with a paid administrator **loses about $7,654 a month** (-34.1% margin) and cannot break even at any occupancy, because its break-even is 119.3%. A 6-bed home only works if the owner is the administrator, and even then the rough arithmetic still shows a loss. Several of these inputs, including PCH staffing under the May 2025 rule amendments, are unverified. Read the financial narrative before committing to a lease.
sections.service_model:
**Who is served.** Georgia personal care homes provide housing, food service and personal services to two or more adults who are not related to the owner or administrator [S14]. Assisted living communities are PCHs of 25 or more residents that hold DCH's permission to provide assisted living care [S1]. A community may not serve more residents than the licensed capacity on the face of its permit [S1]. The Medicaid waiver targets frail elderly and disabled Georgians who would otherwise qualify for nursing facility care [S21]. Private-pay residents are the modeled revenue.

**Two licenses, two rulebooks.** Chapter 111-8-62 governs PCHs of 2 to 24 beds, and Chapter 111-8-63 governs ALCs of 25 or more [S9][S1][S16]. The jump from 24 to 25 beds is the biggest regulatory step in the state. At 25 or more beds the administrator must hold a Board of Long-Term Care Facility Administrators license [S10], and the application needs a DCH Office of Health Planning Letter of Determination and a CPA financial stability affidavit [S4][S1]. The ALC staffing rule adds two on-site direct care staff around the clock and RN/LPN hours on site [S5]. A secondary source says PCHs under 25 beds need no certificate of need [S17]. That has not been verified against DCH's certificate of need rules.

**How the model reflects this.** The model has five configurations: 6-, 12-, 16- and 24-bed PCHs, plus a 30-bed ALC. All are 100% private pay. The PCH configurations are priced at $4,395 because a shared room in a residential home likely prices below the private one-bedroom benchmark [S48][S30]. The ALC is priced at $5,300 for private units [S30].

**Memory care.** Communities operating memory care centers must hold a DCH certification [S19]. The fee is $200 a year [S3]. The ALC packet says you must hold a current ALC permit before applying [S4], so confirm with DCH whether a PCH can apply. Memory care is not modeled.
sections.licensing_pathway:
**Regulator and portal.** DCH HFRD licenses both PCHs and ALCs. PCH Program questions go to 404-657-5863 (applications and waivers 404-657-5700, payments 404-651-8155; the DCH main switchboard is (404) 656-4507), and permit, survey and administrator-update questions go to the Personal Care Home Team at pchprogram.hfrd@dch.ga.gov [S8][S4]. ALC applications are filed through the online GAHLES portal, and status correspondence goes to the contact email on the application [S4]. **We did not retrieve a PCH-specific (under 25 beds) application packet.** Use the ALC packet as a guide and confirm the PCH document list with the PCH Team before you spend money on inspections.

**Step by step (ALC packet).**
1. Form the legal entity. If the home is owned by an LLC, the LLC's governing body authorizes the license application [S9].
2. Settle local zoning and location requirements with the responsible local officials [S1].
3. Obtain the DCH Office of Health Planning Letter of Determination [S4].
4. Obtain a notarized CPA Affidavit of Financial Stability (DCH form) attesting that the applicant has demonstrated the financial resources to operate. It is required for ALCs and PCHs of 25 or more beds. The CPA reviews prior-fiscal-year financials or, if there is no history, sufficient documents, which may be forward-looking such as a pro forma [S4][S1].
5. Collect the property documents. These are a floor plan showing windows, doors, common areas and room measurements, plus digital photos of the exterior, common areas and a typical resident room [S1]. You also need a State Fire Marshal inspection report dated within 12 months of submission [S4] and an electrical compliance form from a Georgia-licensed electrician dated within 6 months [S4]. If water is not city or county supplied, you need a private water test dated within 6 months [S4].
6. Complete fingerprint-based GCHEXS background checks for the administrator and for every individual owner with 10% or more interest. The determination letter must be dated within 12 months [S4]. Owners of 10% or more must also be disclosed in the application [S1].
7. Pay the $300 new-application processing fee on submission [S3]. It is non-refundable, and all licensure fees, including the initial license fee, must be paid in full before a permit or license is issued [S4].
8. DCH will not act on an incomplete application [S1]. The DCH checklist states an initial review timeframe of **30 business days** from submission, with applications reviewed in order received [S4]. That figure is in the checklist, not in the rule, and it is an *initial review* period, not a guaranteed approval date. A "90–120 day" timeline from a blog was not confirmed and is not used.
9. The governing body must hold a valid permit before admitting any residents [S1]. Permits cannot be transferred between communities or locations, and they cease to be valid on a change of ownership [S2].

**Fees (DCH schedule, Oct 2024).** The new application fee is $300 on submission. The annual license fee is $350 for a PCH of 2 to 24 beds, $750 for an ALC of 25 to 50 beds, and $1,500 for an ALC of 51 or more beds. The initial license fee ($350 PCH 2–24 beds, $750 ALC 25–50 beds) is submitted before the license is issued. A late fee of $150 applies 60 days past due, a permit replacement is $50, and a memory care certificate is $200 a year [S3]. The Board administrator application is $110 per administrator. Fire-marshal, electrical, zoning, CPA, fingerprint, per-hire screening (fingerprint, TB, physical) and Office of Health Planning costs have no verified official figure; treat any number for them as an operator estimate.

**Administrator.** For homes under 25 beds, the administrator needs an associate's degree, or a GED or high school diploma plus 2 years of licensed PCH or healthcare experience, and must be at least 21 [S10][S13]. At 25 or more beds the administrator must hold a Board license, effective within 60 days of hire [S10]. A Board license has been required for ALC administrators since July 1, 2021 [S7]. The Board application asks for at least one year of full-time experience (1,560 hours in the preceding 12 months) plus a Board-approved administration program, with a $100 application fee and $10 processing fee on the 11.2022 form [S6]. Confirm the current fee with the Board.

**After licensure.** Communities are subject to unannounced periodic inspections, and policies and procedures must be available for review [S4]. A change of ownership of a PCH requires at least 30 days' written notice to DCH and all residents [S9]. DCH presented proposed amendments to Chapter 111-8-62 for initial adoption on 2/13/2025, and their final status was not verified [S12].
sections.reimbursement:
**Private pay is the modeled revenue.** CareScout's 2025 survey (July–November 2025) puts Georgia's assisted living community median at $5,300 a month, $166 a day and $63,600 a year, for a private one-bedroom unit. The U.S. median is $6,200 a month [S30]. For comparison, Georgia nursing homes run $8,821 (semi-private) to $9,429 (private) a month [S30]. A Place for Mom-based reporting lists Georgia's 2026 median at $4,395 a month [S48], and the same site's own page gives $4,752 [S49]. The model uses $4,395 for PCHs and $5,300 for the ALC. No public price source exists for small shared-room homes.

**How Medicaid money flows.** Georgia's Medicaid home- and community-based services for older and disabled adults sit under the Elderly and Disabled Waiver Program, which the state labels as formerly CCSP. CCSP and SOURCE serve people who otherwise qualify for nursing facility care [S20][S21]. Under CCSP, Alternative Living Services means state-licensed personal care homes providing 24-hour personal care supervision [S22]. DFCS Medicaid policy lists it as personal care home placement [S23]. DCH contracts with 12 Area Agencies on Aging to run CCSP statewide, and entry starts with an AAA assessment at 866-552-4464 [S22][S51]. SOURCE also includes personal care home placement [S29]. The official SOURCE page says it is available only in certain areas [S52], and a secondary source says statewide. Check county availability.

**Room and board is resident-paid.** Waiver funding does not pay a resident's room and board in a personal care home [S27]. Two secondary sources say residents pay the home **$768 a month** from SSI, a rate they attribute to the DHS Division of Aging effective January 1, 2026, and keep $226 of the $994 SSI benefit [S24][S25][S26]. No official notice was retrieved. Participants may also owe an income-based cost share to offset the unpaid portion of ALS services [S24][S22].

**What we could not find.** There is no 2026 Medicaid rate for ALS, no HCPCS code or unit definition for ALS itself, and no confirmation of whether claims route fee-for-service or through managed care. GAMMIS says fee-for-service, Georgia Families and Georgia Families 360 coexist [S31], and secondary sources conflict on state-plan personal care. Operators should get the ALS rate and billing path in writing from DCH before relying on Medicaid revenue.

**Program risk.** Admission to CCSP depends on funding appropriated by the legislature [S22]. Georgia's federal share of Elderly and Disabled Waiver costs fell to about 65% per one secondary report [S25], and CMS lists the waiver's current expiration as 11/08/2027 [S50]. A new provider should treat waiver revenue as an upside and not as a plan.
sections.demand:
**Demographics.** U.S. Census QuickFacts shows 16.7% of Georgia's 11,302,748 residents (July 1, 2025 estimate) are 65 or older [S47]. That is roughly 1.9 million people by simple arithmetic. Nursing home private rooms cost $9,429 a month [S30], well above the $4,395–$5,300 assisted living benchmarks [S48][S30]. That price gap is the core reason families look at PCHs and ALCs.

**Supply.** DCH reports 2,910 facilities of mixed types (PCHs, ALCs and other settings) serving about 55,000 residents [S14]. That works out to roughly 19 residents per facility on average, which suggests many small homes. The page is undated, and no count of PCHs vs. ALCs, no county data and no occupancy data were found.

**Referral sources.** The only verified referral channel is the Area Agency on Aging line (866-552-4464), which screens waiver applicants and assigns urgency that affects waitlist placement [S51][S22]. Georgia's waiver guide says there are nearly always people on the waiting lists for the home and community-based waivers. Selection depends on severity of need, informal support and time on the list [S29]. DFCS policy places eligible applicants on the EDWP waiting list [S23]. A secondary source estimates CCSP enrollment takes 2 to 4 months and that residents can move in during the process [S24]. Waitlist length is a reason that private-pay admissions drive the model. Referral-source mix (hospital discharge planners, physicians, families) was not found. Plan a marketing budget and relationship-building with discharge planners and local senior services, but do not assume a referral volume.

**Waiver eligibility context.** The CCSP applicant income limit is 300% of the federal benefit rate. One secondary source gives $2,982 a month for 2026 and another $2,901 [S28][S24]. The individual asset cap is $2,000 per a third-party source. Confirm current limits with DFCS.
sections.operations:
**Staffing rules.** The ALC staffing rule was amended effective May 21, 2025 [S5]. Communities must average at least one awake direct care staff per 15 residents in waking hours and one per 20 in non-waking hours for residents with minimal care needs. At least two on-site direct care staff must be on the premises 24 hours a day whenever residents are present, with one on each occupied floor. At least two fully trained staff must be present at all times [S5]. An RN or LPN must be on site 8 hours a week for 1 to 30 residents and 16 hours a week for 31 to 60 [S5]. For PCHs under 25 beds, the DCH combined-rule text used in this model is 1:15 waking and 1:25 non-waking [S11]. For 25 or more beds the DCH synopsis says 1:15 waking and 1:20 non-waking on an average monthly basis [S12]. **Law-firm reporting says the new staffing rules took effect for both PCHs and ALCs in May 2025 [S18], and we did not verify whether they changed the PCH ratios or added a two-staff minimum for PCHs.** Call the PCH Team before you finalize a schedule.

**Training and health.** The two rulebooks differ. In PCHs (Rule 111-8-62-.09), all direct care staff need at least 16 hours of training per year, with no 24-hour first-year requirement, and emergency first aid and CPR certification within 60 days applies to any person working in the home [S13]. In ALCs (Rule 111-8-63-.09), first aid and CPR within 60 days apply to staff hired to provide hands-on personal services, and those staff, including the administrator, need 24 hours of continuing education in the first year and 16 hours a year after that [S5]. On age: in PCHs, managers and supervisory staff must be at least 21 and non-supervisory hands-on staff at least 18 [S13]. In ALCs, the on-site manager and responsible staff must be at least 21, and staff under 18 may work only with direct line-of-sight supervision, or at age 17 after a Georgia high-school nursing-assistant track [S5]. The administrator and each employee need a TB screening and physical exam within 12 months before providing care [S5]. The administrator must have a satisfactory fingerprint records check before serving [S5]; both rules also require a fingerprint check, TB screen and physical for every direct-access employee.

**Modeled staffing.** The model uses one awake direct care staff member around the clock (730 hrs/month) in every PCH. It adds a second aide for 8 hours a day at 12 beds, and a second awake staff member for 16 hours a day at 16 and 24 beds. The 24-bed home adds a third staff member at 40 hrs/week. The model includes cook/housekeeping hours, a nurse consultant (4 hrs/week at 6 and 12 beds, 8 hrs/week at 16 and 24 beds), and an administrator salary ($55,000 for 6, 12 and 16 beds; $60,000 at 24 beds). The 30-bed ALC has two awake staff 24/7, a third for 16 hours a day, 8 hrs/week of RN/LPN, 2.5 FTE of cook/housekeeping, 0.5 FTE activities, and a $75,000 Board-licensed administrator. Hours above the rule minimums, the PCH nurse hours and all administrator salaries are operator estimates.

**Systems.** Georgia EVV applies to Medicaid personal care services. Mandatory EVV claim submission applies to applicable HHCS claims with dates of service on or after September 14, 2026, through Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+ [S32]. No Medicaid revenue is modeled, so no EVV cost is included. The model carries a $250 a month eMAR/documentation software estimate. Providers who have not revalidated with GAMMIS by July 1, 2026 are suspended, and retroactive Medicaid enrollment is not permitted [S31].
sections.market_conditions:
**Pricing.** Georgia's CareScout median of $5,300 is below the U.S. median of $6,200 [S30]. The $4,395 A Place for Mom-based median [S48] is lower, and $4,752 on another page of the same site [S49] shows the benchmarks disagree. These surveys measure assisted living communities, not small shared-room PCHs, and the $4,395 median covers all Georgia assisted living move-ins. The CareScout survey window (July–November 2025) predates full-year 2026 pricing [S30]. Set your price from three to five local comparables.

**Labor.** The Atlanta MSA mean hourly wage for the personal care and service group was $18.17 and for food preparation and serving $15.37 (May 2025) [S41]. These are group means used as proxies for caregivers and kitchen staff, not occupation-specific Georgia wages. The statewide OEWS page could not be fetched. National medians from BLS (May 2025) are $42,260 a year for nursing assistants, $39,490 for nursing assistants in assisted living and continuing care settings, $35,800 for home health and personal care aides, and $97,550 for registered nurses [S42][S43][S44]. The model uses the RN national median ($46.90/hr) for the nurse line because no Georgia or LPN wage was found; this mixes a national RN median with Atlanta means. The federal minimum wage of $7.25 applies. Georgia's own $5.15 minimum covers employers of six or more but yields to the federal rate [S34]. No higher local metro minimum wage was found, and a secondary source says local rates are not allowed [S35]. This was not verified against a statute. Modeled wages are well above $7.25. Wages in Atlanta may be higher or lower than in other parts of the state.

**Real estate.** Rent uses HUD FY2026 Fair Market Rents for the Atlanta-Sandy Springs-Roswell HMFA: $1,585 studio, $1,660 one bedroom, $1,820 two bedroom, $2,182 three bedroom and $2,605 four bedroom [S45]. HUD's FY2027 FMRs took effect Oct 1, 2026, so these FY2026 values are superseded. A secondary source reports the Atlanta four-bedroom at $2,493 (about $2,867 on the same 1.15 markup) and the two-bedroom at $1,762 [S46]. The model keeps the FY2026 values, so modeled rent may be somewhat high. PCH rent is the four-bedroom FMR × 1.15 for a five-bedroom home ($2,996) at about $499 per licensed bed, scaled to bed count. The ALC uses 30 studio units at $1,585 ($47,550). These are floors that exclude common areas, and real commercial rent could differ. Get real quotes.

**Taxes and fees.** Georgia's new-employer unemployment rate is 2.70% on a $9,500 wage base [S36]. Federal FUTA (about $42 per employee a year) is not in the model. An LLC costs $110 to form and about $60 a year to maintain (another secondary source lists a $50 base fee) [S37][S38]. One secondary source says Georgia has no LLC franchise tax [S39]. A local occupational tax certificate is typically required and ranges from $10 to $1,000+ depending on locality [S40].
sections.financial_narrative:
**How the P&L is built.** Revenue per resident is the private-pay monthly fee ($4,395 for the PCH configurations [S48], $5,300 for the ALC [S30]). Staffing is built bed-by-bed from the rule minimums plus operator choices, with payroll burden of 8.5% payroll tax (FICA plus SUI [S36]), 4% workers' comp and 3% benefits. The last two are operator estimates. Rent, base utilities and the license fee are fixed and sized to licensed beds, because vacant beds still cost rent. Food, supplies, insurance, activities and referral fees scale with census. Occupancy defaults to 85% (75% conservative, 92% optimistic) as an operator planning assumption, since no Georgia occupancy data was found.

**Results at 85% occupancy.**

| Configuration | Net/month | Margin | Break-even occupancy | First profit month | Cash needed (rough) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 24-bed PCH | $19,025 | 21.2% | 63.7% | 6 | $142,027 |
| 30-bed ALC | $6,611 | 4.9% | 80.2% | 10 | $435,837 |
| 16-bed PCH | $4,040 | 6.8% | 78.2% | 8 | $148,793 |
| 12-bed PCH | $1,257 | 2.8% | 82.2% | 12 | $194,867 |
| 6-bed PCH (paid administrator) | -$7,654 | -34.1% | 119.3% (cannot break even) | none | $322,977 |

The cash-needed figures have not been reconciled to the full startup list (application and license fees, Board application, fingerprint checks, per-hire screening, inspections, water test, CPA affidavit, zoning) and include operator estimates. Treat them as rough.

**Why size matters.** The fixed costs are one awake staff member around the clock (730 hrs), an administrator, a nurse consultant and rent. A 6-bed home spreads them over at most 6 residents at $4,395 a month. At 85% that is about 5.1 residents and roughly $22,400 of revenue against costs the model puts around $30,000. The 24-bed PCH earns much more per resident because the first awake staff member and the administrator are shared by many more residents. It breaks even at about 15 residents (63.7% × 24 = 15.3). The 12-bed home breaks even at about 10 residents (82.2% × 12 = 9.9), and 85% of 12 is 10.2, so **one fewer resident takes the home below break-even**. The 16-bed home breaks even at about 13 residents (12.5). The 30-bed ALC breaks even at about 25 residents (24.1) against 25.5 at 85%, so it has almost no cushion. At the 75% conservative case the 12-bed, 16-bed and 30-bed models lose money, and the 24-bed model stays profitable because its break-even is 63.7%.

**The 6-bed home.** At 100% occupancy the 6-bed home takes in $26,370 a month (6 × $4,395) against about $30,700 of listed costs, a loss of about $4,300 a month before any vacancy. It is structurally unprofitable at the $4,395 benchmark, which is a median for all Georgia assisted living move-ins and not a small-PCH price. The model puts an administrator salary of $55,000 a year in this home. If the owner is the administrator and takes no other pay, that is about $4,600 a month before burden. By rough arithmetic (not a model run) the home would still lose roughly $2,400 to $3,100 a month. A 6-bed PCH is not viable on these rent and staffing inputs unless the owner owns the property, the owner provides much of the care, or the price is well above $4,395. Treat any 6-bed pitch skeptically.

**The ALC is not an automatic upgrade.** The 30-bed ALC earns a higher price ($5,300), but it needs a Board-licensed administrator, the Letter of Determination, the CPA affidavit, two awake staff around the clock, RN/LPN hours and a studio-per-unit rent floor of $47,550 a month. It leaves only a 4.9% margin and needs about $435,837 in cash. The rent basis differs from the PCH models (a shared-room per-bed estimate vs. studio units), so the two are not a clean like-for-like comparison. Do not assume that going from 24 to 25+ beds raises profit.

**Sensitivities (simple arithmetic, not model runs).**
- **Price.** At 85% of 24 beds (20.4 residents), each $100 on the monthly fee is about $2,040 a month. A 10% cut in the $4,395 fee costs about $9,000 a month, which leaves the 24-bed PCH profitable. For the 16-bed home (13.6 residents), each $100 is about $1,360, and a 10% cut turns it into a loss.
- **Wages.** The model's $18.17 is an Atlanta group mean. If caregiver wages are $2 an hour higher, the 24-bed home's roughly 1,390 hours of direct care add about $3,200 a month after the 15.5% burden. The 16-bed home's roughly 1,217 hours add about $2,800, which eliminates most of its $4,040 net.
- **Staffing rule risk.** If DCH reads the May 2025 amendments to require two awake staff around the clock in PCHs [S18], the extra cost at $18.17/hr and 15.5% burden is about $5,100 a month for the 16- and 24-bed homes (243 more hours), about $10,200 for the 12-bed home, and about $15,300 for the 6-bed home. That would cut the 24-bed net to roughly $13,900, push the 16-bed to about -$1,100 and the 12-bed to about -$9,000. Verify this before signing a lease.
- **Rent.** PCH rent is an HUD-derived estimate for Atlanta, based on FY2026 FMRs that are now superseded by FY2027 (a secondary source shows a lower 4BR figure). Rural Georgia is likely cheaper, but commercial space for 24 beds could cost more. Get local quotes.

**What is excluded.** The model excludes Medicaid revenue, owner income tax, federal FUTA and loan payments. Startup costs and the working-capital deficit are in the cash-needed figures, but those figures are not reconciled to the full startup list. Fire-marshal, electrical, fingerprint, per-hire screening, CPA affidavit, Letter of Determination and zoning costs have no verified official figure and are operator estimates. The path to profit is a 24-bed home (or a 16-bed home with a strong referral pipeline), owner-operated where possible, filled quickly and priced from local comparables.
sections.risks:
- **Staffing rule uncertainty.** PCH staffing under the May 21, 2025 amendments was not verified [S18][S5]. A two-staff minimum for PCHs would add about $5,100 to $15,300 a month depending on size (see financial narrative), and could turn the 16-bed and 12-bed models negative.
- **Occupancy.** Small homes swing on one resident. The 12-bed model's break-even (about 10 residents) is almost the same as its 85% census (10.2). The 30-bed ALC needs about 25 residents and is modeled at 25.5. No Georgia occupancy data was found.
- **Pricing.** Benchmarks are for AL communities, not small shared-room homes [S30][S48]. Sources disagree ($4,395 vs. $4,752) [S48][S49]. A lower price can push most models below break-even.
- **Wages.** Modeled wages are Atlanta group means [S41]. Nursing assistant medians nationally are higher [S42]. Local minimum-wage claims were not verified, but modeled wages are well above $7.25 [S34][S35]. Tight labor markets raise turnover and training cost, and the 60-day first aid/CPR deadline and annual training hours (16 a year in PCHs; 24 in the first year for ALC hands-on staff) still apply [S5][S13].
- **Licensing and permit.** An application is not acted on until complete [S1]. The 30-business-day review is a checklist figure, not a rule deadline [S4]. You cannot admit anyone before the permit is issued [S1], so rent and payroll run through the wait. Permits do not transfer and end on an ownership change [S2], and a change of ownership needs 30 days' written notice [S9]. The owner's or administrator's background check can delay the file [S4].
- **ALC prerequisites.** The Letter of Determination, the CPA Affidavit of Financial Stability and the Board administrator license add cost and time [S4][S1][S6]. The certificate-of-need position for expansions is unverified [S17].
- **Rule changes.** DCH presented amendments to Chapter 111-8-62 on 2/13/2025, and final adoption was not verified [S12]. Watch DCH Board actions [S16].
- **Medicaid dependence.** Waiver admission depends on legislative funding and waitlists are nearly always present [S22][S29]. The federal share is about 65% per a secondary source [S25], and the waiver's current term expires 11/08/2027 [S50]. No ALS rate was found. Medicaid residents pay $768 room and board from SSI [S24], so a Medicaid bed would earn far less than private pay, and its economics are unverified.
- **Insurance and workers' compensation.** No DCH insurance minimum or Georgia workers' comp loss-cost data was found. The model's $100 per resident and 4% estimates are not quotes.
- **Cash.** Rough cash needed ranges from about $142,027 (24-bed) to $435,837 (30-bed ALC), and the 6-bed home needs $322,977 and never turns profitable [model]. These figures are not reconciled to the full startup list and include operator estimates. A ramp that is slower than modeled burns cash faster.
- **Real estate.** Rents are HUD-derived estimates based on superseded FY2026 FMRs, and the ALC figure excludes common areas [S45]. Zoning approval for larger homes is addressed with local officials and not guaranteed [S1].
sections.recommendations:
1. **Pick the size on the numbers.** Do not open a 6-bed PCH with a paid administrator. It loses about $7,654 a month and cannot break even [model]. The 12-bed PCH earns only $1,257 a month and fails at 75% occupancy. The strongest result is the 24-bed PCH ($19,025 a month, 63.7% break-even, first profit month 6, $142,027 cash). A 16-bed PCH is a reasonable stepping stone if you have a referral pipeline and a lower-rent building. It nets $4,040, breaks even at 78.2% and loses at 75%.

2. **Stay at 24 beds unless you have a reason to be an ALC.** Going to 25 or more beds adds a Board-licensed administrator, the Letter of Determination, the CPA affidavit and the 24/7 two-staff plus nurse-hour rules [S10][S4][S1][S5]. The 30-bed ALC nets only $6,611 a month (4.9%) and needs about $435,837 in cash. Consider an ALC only if you have a purpose-built building, a reliable private-pay market at or above $5,300 [S30], and an administrator who already holds a Board license.

3. **Resolve the staffing question before you sign a lease.** Ask the PCH Team (pchprogram.hfrd@dch.ga.gov) in writing which ratios and minimum staffing apply to your bed count after the May 2025 amendments [S8][S4][S18]. Re-run the schedule at both answers.

4. **Own the administrator role if you can.** Under 25 beds the administrator needs an associate's degree, or a GED/diploma plus 2 years of PCH or healthcare experience, and must be 21 or older [S10][S13]. An owner who qualifies saves the $55,000–$60,000 salary line. Do not count on this making a 6-bed home profitable.

5. **Price from local comparables and test the downside.** Check 3–5 local PCH and AL prices. Use $4,395 as a starting reference for shared rooms and $5,300 for private units [S48][S30]. Make sure your plan still works at the 75% conservative case and at a price 10% lower.

6. **Sequence the permit work to protect cash.** Run the zoning conversation first [S1]. Order the fire-marshal report (valid 12 months), the electrical form (6 months) and any water test (6 months) so they are dated within the windows when you submit [S4]. Start GCHEXS checks early [S4]. Submit a complete packet in GAHLES with the $300 fee [S3][S4]. Tie your lease to the permit, because permits do not transfer [S2].

7. **Treat Medicaid as a later option.** Before pursuing the waiver, get the ALS rate and billing path in writing from DCH, enroll in GAMMIS (no retroactive enrollment) [S31], budget the $750 CY2026 enrollment fee if it applies [S33], and plan EVV [S32]. Know that the resident's $768 room and board comes from SSI [S24] and that waiver admission is funding-limited [S22].

8. **Build for referrals.** Make the Area Agency on Aging line (866-552-4464) and local hospital discharge planners part of your marketing [S51]. Private-pay residents are your modeled revenue, so a steady admission pace matters more than any one referral source.

9. **Track the break-even every month.** Compare actual census with the break-even for your size (about 15 residents at 24 beds, 13 at 16 beds, 10 at 12 beds, 25 at 30 beds). Do not raise your plan's price or drop a required cost to make the model profit. If the census runs below break-even for more than a few months, cut fixed costs or add private-pay admissions, not required staffing.

checklist.task: Decide between a Personal Care Home (2–24 beds) and an Assisted Living Community (25+ beds)
checklist.instructions: A PCH is licensed under Rule 111-8-62 (2–24 beds). An ALC is a personal care home serving 25 or more residents that is licensed to provide assisted living care under Rule 111-8-63. The 25-bed threshold changes your administrator licensing, application documents and staffing. Read both chapters before you pick a size.

checklist.task: Confirm what care your license lets you provide
checklist.instructions: A home licensed only as a personal care home may not provide assisted living care unless it holds an ALC license. Ask the DCH PCH Team to confirm in writing which services and resident care levels fit your planned license, and plan admission criteria around the answer.

checklist.task: Choose the size from the pro forma
checklist.instructions: Use the Pro Forma P&L. At 85% occupancy the 24-bed PCH is the strongest model, the 6-bed home with a paid administrator loses money, and the 12-bed, 16-bed and 30-bed ALC models are thin. Re-run with your own rent, price and wages.

checklist.task: Decide on your payer strategy (private pay vs. Medicaid waiver)
checklist.instructions: The model is 100% private pay because no 2026 Medicaid per-diem for Alternative Living Services was found. Medicaid waiver residents pay room and board from SSI and the waiver covers services. Decide whether to pursue the waiver after the home is licensed and full.

checklist.task: List every owner of 10% or more
checklist.instructions: Owners holding 10 percent or more of the corporate stock or ownership must be disclosed in the permit application, along with the registered agent. Each individual 10% owner also needs a GCHEXS fingerprint check. Settle ownership percentages before you apply.

checklist.task: Form the legal entity (LLC) with the Georgia Secretary of State
checklist.instructions: A secondary source lists $110 to form a Georgia LLC ($100 filing plus $10 service charge). Verify the current fee with the Secretary of State. If an LLC owns the home, its governing body authorizes the DCH license application and the LLC is the licensee, so the name must match across all documents.
checklist.cite: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62; Georgia Secretary of State

checklist.task: Calendar the LLC annual registration
checklist.instructions: The annual registration is due April 1. One secondary source says $60 all-in ($50 plus a $10 service charge) and another lists a $50 base fee. Missing April 1 adds a $25 late fee per one source. Confirm the fee with the Secretary of State.
checklist.cite: Georgia Secretary of State annual registration

checklist.task: Confirm entity tax treatment with a CPA
checklist.instructions: One secondary source says Georgia imposes no franchise tax on LLCs and that LLC profits are taxed on the owners' returns. Ask a CPA to confirm, and to advise on owner income tax, which the pro forma excludes.

checklist.task: Obtain an EIN and register with the Georgia Department of Labor for unemployment insurance
checklist.instructions: Apply for an EIN through the IRS. Register with GDOL once you hire. New employers are assigned a total rate of 2.70% on a $9,500 taxable wage base per employee. Add the employer share of FICA (7.65% statutory; not retrieved in this research, so verify).

checklist.task: Obtain the local occupational tax certificate (business license)
checklist.instructions: A secondary source says a local occupational tax certificate is nearly universal and ranges from $10 to $1,000+ depending on locality. Ask your city or county for the schedule. The pro forma carries $25 a month as an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Get insurance quotes (general and professional liability, property, workers' compensation)
checklist.instructions: No DCH insurance minimum or bond requirement for PCH/ALC licensure was found in the sources reviewed, but landlords and lenders usually require coverage and Georgia employers must handle workers' compensation. The pro forma uses an operator estimate of $100 per resident per month and 4% of payroll for workers' comp. Replace them with real quotes.

checklist.task: Plan startup cash and a working-capital reserve
checklist.instructions: The model's cash needed ranges from about $142,027 for the 24-bed PCH to about $435,837 for the 30-bed ALC, and $322,977 for the 6-bed home. You pay rent and payroll before the first resident arrives because you cannot admit anyone before the permit. For an ALC, a CPA must affirm your ability to operate as a going concern for two years.

checklist.task: Resolve zoning and location with local officials before signing a lease
checklist.instructions: The rules say local zoning and location requirements must be addressed by the applicant with the responsible local officials. Get written zoning confirmation for the bed count you plan, since larger homes are likelier to need approval.

checklist.task: Benchmark rent before you sign
checklist.instructions: The pro forma uses HUD FY2026 Atlanta HMFA Fair Market Rents ($1,585 studio to $2,605 four-bedroom) to size rent. A secondary source reports the FY2027 two-bedroom FMR falling to $1,762. Use real quotes for your market. Rent is fixed, and vacant beds still cost money.

checklist.task: Make the lease depend on the license
checklist.instructions: Permits are not transferable between locations and cease to be valid when ownership changes. Negotiate lease terms that let you exit, or delay rent, if DCH denies the permit or the fire or electrical inspections fail.

checklist.task: Prepare an accurate floor plan
checklist.instructions: The application requires a floor plan showing windows, doors, common areas and resident room measurements. Prepare it from a measured survey of the actual building.

checklist.task: Take digital photos of the exterior, common areas and a typical resident room
checklist.instructions: The application requires digital photos (.jpg format). Take them when the building is furnished and ready.

checklist.task: Order the State Fire Marshal inspection
checklist.instructions: The ALC application requires a fire marshal inspection report showing no violations and the capacity load. It must be dated within 12 months of application submission. Fire inspection fees were not verified. Confirm the PCH document list with the PCH Team.

checklist.task: Get the electrical compliance form signed by a Georgia-licensed electrician
checklist.instructions: The form must be dated within 6 months of the application submission date. Schedule it close to submission so it does not expire. Fees were not verified.

checklist.task: Test private water if not on a city or county system
checklist.instructions: A private water test is required when water is not supplied by a city or county system. It must be dated within 6 months of submission.

checklist.task: Set your licensed capacity
checklist.instructions: The community may not serve more residents than the approved licensed capacity on the face of the permit. Decide bed count (and the 24 vs. 25 threshold) before you apply, because capacity drives fees, administrator requirements and staffing.

checklist.task: Meet or call DCH early
checklist.instructions: Call (404) 656-4507 or email pchprogram.hfrd@dch.ga.gov to confirm the PCH application packet and any building requirements for your bed count. Visiting address: 2 Martin Luther King Jr. Drive SE, East Tower, Atlanta, GA 30334 (Mon–Fri, 8 a.m.–5 p.m. ET).

checklist.task: Choose a qualified administrator (homes under 25 beds)
checklist.instructions: For homes licensed for fewer than 25 beds the administrator needs an associate's degree, or a GED or high school diploma plus 2 years of licensed PCH or healthcare experience, and must be at least 21. If you are the owner and qualify, you can fill the role yourself.

checklist.task: Secure a Board-licensed administrator (ALC, or any home of 25+ beds)
checklist.instructions: Homes licensed for 25 or more beds must have an administrator who holds a license from the State Board of Long-Term Care Facility Administrators, effective within 60 days of hire. Administrators of ALCs have needed a Board license since July 1, 2021.

checklist.task: Prepare the Board administrator application
checklist.instructions: The 11.2022 form requires at least one year of full-time practical or managerial experience (1,560 hours in the preceding 12 months) plus a Board-approved administration program, with a $100 application fee and $10 processing fee payable to the Board. Confirm the current fee with the Board.
checklist.cite: Board of Long-Term Care Facility Administrators application

checklist.task: Complete the administrator's fingerprint background check
checklist.instructions: The administrator must obtain a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination before serving. For the ALC application, the GCHEXS determination letter must be dated within 12 months.

checklist.task: Complete GCHEXS background checks for all 10%+ individual owners
checklist.instructions: All administrators and individual owners with 10% or more ownership interest must complete a fingerprint-based background check through GCHEXS. Start early because the application cannot be acted on without it.

checklist.task: Check staff age rules
checklist.instructions: On-site managers and direct-care supervisory staff must be at least 21. Non-supervisory staff providing hands-on care must be at least 18.

checklist.task: Confirm minimum staffing for your bed count with DCH
checklist.instructions: PCHs under 25 beds: 1 awake direct care staff per 15 residents waking, 1 per 25 non-waking (from an undated DCH combined-rule text). ALCs: 1 per 15 waking and 1 per 20 non-waking, at least 2 on-site direct care staff 24 hours a day with one on each occupied floor. New staffing rules took effect May 21, 2025 for PCHs and ALCs. Whether they changed the PCH ratios was not verified, so ask the PCH Team.

checklist.task: Plan RN/LPN hours (ALC)
checklist.instructions: A registered nurse or LPN must be on site at least 8 hours a week for communities with 1 to 30 residents and 16 hours a week for 31 to 60 residents. The model uses a nurse consultant for PCHs as an operator choice, since the nurse rule was verified for ALCs only.

checklist.task: Build a staff schedule with at least two fully trained staff present (ALC)
checklist.instructions: At least two fully trained staff must be present at all times any residents are present, with one on each occupied floor. Build coverage for call-outs and vacation, not only the minimum.

checklist.task: Set wages and check minimum-wage compliance
checklist.instructions: The federal $7.25 minimum applies (Georgia's $5.15 applies to employers of 6+ but yields to the federal rate). The model uses Atlanta MSA group means ($18.17 personal care and service; $15.37 food preparation and serving) as proxies. Check local pay for aides, cooks and nurses before you hire.
checklist.cite: DOL State Minimum Wage Laws; BLS Atlanta MSA May 2025

checklist.task: Collect TB screening and physical exam for every employee
checklist.instructions: The administrator and each employee must have a TB screening and physical exam within 12 months before providing care to residents.

checklist.task: Schedule initial staff training within 60 days of hire
checklist.instructions: Every new staff member must receive work-related training within the first 60 days of employment, including emergency first aid and CPR certification.

checklist.task: Track continuing education hours
checklist.instructions: Staff providing hands-on care, including the administrator, need 24 hours of continuing education in the first year of employment and at least 16 hours of job-related continuing education annually after that. Keep a training log by employee.

checklist.task: Set up payroll and payroll tax accounts
checklist.instructions: Plan for GDOL unemployment tax (2.70% on $9,500 for new employers), FICA and workers' compensation. The model carries 8.5% payroll tax, 4% workers' comp and 3% benefits. The last two are operator estimates, so replace them with a carrier quote.

checklist.task: Obtain the DCH Office of Health Planning Letter of Determination
checklist.instructions: The initial ALC application requires a Letter of Determination approved by the DCH Office of Health Planning. Fee and process were not verified, so contact DCH early. A secondary source says PCHs under 25 beds need no certificate of need.

checklist.task: Obtain a CPA financial stability affidavit
checklist.instructions: The initial application must include an affidavit from a certified public accountant affirming the applicant's ability to operate as a going concern for the next two years. Prepare a two-year budget with a CPA. The fee was not verified.

checklist.task: Complete the Affidavit of Compliance
checklist.instructions: The packet includes an affidavit acknowledging that after licensure the community is subject to unannounced periodic inspections and that policies and procedures must be available for review. Complete it with the application.

checklist.task: Work through the full DCH ALC application checklist
checklist.instructions: Use the DCH checklist (updated 07/13/26) as your master document list and tick off each attachment before you submit.

checklist.task: Confirm the PCH application packet with the PCH Team (homes under 25 beds)
checklist.instructions: A PCH-specific packet was not retrieved in this research. Ask DCH for the current PCH application checklist, and confirm which ALC documents (Letter of Determination, CPA affidavit, fire, electrical, water) apply to your PCH.
checklist.cite: DCH HFRD Personal Care Home Program

checklist.task: Create your GAHLES portal account and file online
checklist.instructions: ALC applications are filed through the online application portal at https://gahles.dch.georgia.gov/. Status correspondence goes to the contact email on the application, so use a monitored address.

checklist.task: Pay the $300 new-application processing fee
checklist.instructions: The new application processing fee is $300 on submission. It is non-refundable.
checklist.cite: DCH Schedule of Licensure Activity Fees

checklist.task: Submit a complete application
checklist.instructions: DCH will not act on an application unless it has been determined complete with all required attachments and fees. Check every item twice before you submit.

checklist.task: Plan for the 30-business-day initial review
checklist.instructions: The DCH checklist states an initial review timeframe of 30 business days from submission, with applications reviewed in order received. This is a checklist figure, not a rule deadline, and not a total time to a permit. Budget rent and payroll for a longer wait.

checklist.task: Pay the initial license fee before the permit is issued
checklist.instructions: The initial license fee is submitted before license issuance, and all licensure fees must be paid in full before a permit or license is issued. Annual fee: $350 (PCH 2–24 beds), $750 (ALC 25–50 beds), $1,500 (ALC 51+ beds).
checklist.cite: DCH Schedule of Licensure Activity Fees

checklist.task: Avoid late fees
checklist.instructions: A $150 late fee applies per instance 60 days past due. Pay renewals on time and track the due dates.
checklist.cite: DCH Schedule of Licensure Activity Fees

checklist.task: Do not admit any resident before the permit is issued
checklist.instructions: The governing body must hold a valid permit from the Department before admitting any residents (and, for PCHs, before operating). Do not take deposits for move-in dates you cannot guarantee.

checklist.task: Post and file the permit; know the replacement fee
checklist.instructions: Keep the permit with your licensed capacity visible and on file. A permit replacement costs $50 per request.
checklist.cite: DCH Schedule of Licensure Activity Fees

checklist.task: Write policies and procedures and keep them available
checklist.instructions: Communities are subject to unannounced periodic inspections at which policies and procedures must be available for review. Keep a current binder or digital copy accessible on site.

checklist.task: Set admission criteria that match your license
checklist.instructions: A PCH may not provide assisted living care. Write admission and discharge criteria based on what your permit allows, and train staff to apply them.

checklist.task: Set your private-pay rate from local comparables
checklist.instructions: Benchmarks: CareScout 2025 Georgia assisted living median $5,300 a month (private one-bedroom in an AL community; U.S. $6,200); A Place for Mom-based 2026 median $4,395 (a second page of the same site says $4,752). Neither measures small shared-room homes. Survey 3–5 local competitors.

checklist.task: Build a medication management plan with a nurse
checklist.instructions: Arrange nurse oversight hours (ALC rule: 8 hrs/week for 1–30 residents, 16 hrs/week for 31–60). Confirm what medication tasks your staff may perform under your license before you admit residents who need them.

checklist.task: Choose eMAR / documentation software
checklist.instructions: The model carries $250 a month as an operator estimate. Georgia EVV applies to Medicaid personal care billing, so no EVV cost is modeled without Medicaid revenue.

checklist.task: Set up a marketing and referral plan
checklist.instructions: Introduce the home to hospital discharge planners, physicians and the Area Agency on Aging network (866-552-4464). Referral-source mix was not found, so test channels and track where residents come from.

checklist.task: Track monthly occupancy against break-even
checklist.instructions: Model break-evens at 85% occupancy: 24-bed PCH 63.7%, 16-bed 78.2%, 12-bed 82.2%, 30-bed ALC 80.2%. Review census monthly and act early if you run below your size's break-even.

checklist.task: Understand how Alternative Living Services works
checklist.instructions: Under CCSP, Alternative Living Services means state-licensed personal care homes providing 24-hour personal care supervision. DFCS policy calls it personal care home placement. The waiver pays for services, not room and board.

checklist.task: Get the ALS rate and billing path in writing before you plan on Medicaid
checklist.instructions: No 2026 ALS per-diem, code or unit definition was found, and whether claims run fee-for-service or through managed care was not confirmed. Ask DCH and the Area Agency on Aging, and treat Medicaid as an upside until you have a rate.

checklist.task: Enroll as a Georgia Medicaid provider in GAMMIS
checklist.instructions: Retroactive enrollment is not permitted, so dates of service before enrollment are not payable. Providers who had not revalidated by July 1, 2026 are suspended. Confirm what applies to a new PCH.

checklist.task: Budget the CY2026 enrollment application fee if it applies
checklist.instructions: The CY2026 federal Medicare/Medicaid/CHIP application fee is $750, charged to institutional providers at initial enrollment, revalidation or new location. Whether PCH/ALS waiver providers are classed as institutional was not confirmed in an official Georgia source.

checklist.task: Plan for EVV if you bill waiver personal support services
checklist.instructions: DCH selected Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+ as the state EVV system. Mandatory EVV submission applies to applicable HHCS claims with dates of service on or after September 14, 2026. The EVV code table lists CCSP/SOURCE personal support services under T1019. ALS codes were not verified.

checklist.task: Know the resident's room-and-board contribution and cost share
checklist.instructions: Two secondary sources say waiver residents pay a personal care home $768 a month (from $994 SSI) effective January 1, 2026, and keep $226. Residents may also owe an income-based cost share. Verify with DHS and DFCS.

checklist.task: Expect waitlists and funding limits
checklist.instructions: CCSP admission depends on legislative funding, and Georgia's waiver guide says there are nearly always people on the waiting lists. Applicants start with an AAA assessment at 866-552-4464. Secondary reporting estimates 2–4 months from start to finish.
checklist.cite: CCSP fact sheet; Medicaid waiver guide

checklist.task: Watch waiver term and funding risk
checklist.instructions: CMS lists the Elderly and Disabled Waiver current expiration as 11/08/2027, and one secondary report says the federal share fell to about 65%. Do not make a business plan depend on waiver revenue.

startup_costs.notes: $350 for a PCH of 2–24 beds; $750 for an ALC of 25–50 beds.

startup_costs.item: Board of Long-Term Care Facility Administrators application
startup_costs.notes: Needed for each administrator of a 25+ bed home or ALC. Figure is from the 11.2022 form; confirm the current fee with the Board.

startup_costs.item: GCHEXS fingerprint checks for the administrator and each owner with 10%+ interest
startup_costs.notes: Required for the ALC application. No official fee figure was retrieved.

startup_costs.item: Per-hire fingerprint check, TB screen and physical for every direct-access employee
startup_costs.notes: Required by Rules 111-8-62-.09 and 111-8-63-.09. No official cost figure was retrieved.

Electrical compliance form from a Georgia-licensed electrician (dated within 6 months)
Water test (if not on city or county water) or septic test

startup_costs.notes: Required for ALCs and PCHs of 25+ beds. CPA fee not found.

Fees vary by county or city.
